meta.title: Flex Ltd — Revathi Advaithi's diversified EMS pivot toward AI data centre power and infrastructure assembly
meta.abstract: Flex Ltd is a Singapore-headquartered electronics manufacturing services (EMS) and supply chain solutions company listed on the NASDAQ under the ticker FLEX. The company traces its origins to 1969 when Flextronics International was founded; the modern Flex organisation reflects multi-decade strategic evolution including the November 2015 corporate rebrand from Flextronics to Flex Ltd. The company operates three reporting segments: Flex Agility Solutions (FAS, covering consumer, communications, and lifestyle product categories), Flex Reliability Solutions (FRS, covering automotive, health solutions, and industrial categories), and Nextracker (the solar tracker business that was spun off via IPO in February 2023, with Flex completing the full separation by January 2024). Under CEO Revathi Advaithi (since February 2019, succeeding Mike McNamara), the strategic mandate has been the higher-margin product and customer category emphasis, the Nextracker separation completion, and the broader strategic posture refinement toward the AI data centre infrastructure assembly opportunity plus the broader high-mix high-complexity manufacturing positioning. The fiscal 2024 revenue was approximately $26.4 billion reflecting the broader multi-segment scaling combined with the Nextracker separation impact; the fiscal 2025 revenue was approximately $25.8 billion reflecting the continued multi-segment trajectory. The AI data centre infrastructure assembly opportunity has emerged as a meaningful incremental growth driver within the Flex Reliability Solutions segment scaling.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
After the January 2024 full separation of Nextracker (NASDAQ: NXT), Flex Ltd (FLEX, NASDAQ) stood as the largest US-public-listed electronics manufacturing services supplier by revenue — a clean-sheet franchise anchored in Singapore by charter, operationally headquartered in Austin, Texas, and led by President and CEO Revathi Advaithi since February 2019. The separation, preceded by Nextracker's February 2023 IPO, stripped away the solar-tracker business that had inflated the FY2023 revenue line to $30.0 billion and clarified the company's identity as a diversified industrial EMS franchise with a sharpening orientation toward higher-margin, longer-cycle product categories. By the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, Flex was executing a second, structurally analogous resequencing — the planned separation of its Cloud and Power Infrastructure business — that compressed two strategic cycles into a single CEO tenure.

Advaithi succeeded long-tenured CEO Mike McNamara carrying the operating credentials of a two-decade Eaton Corporation career that culminated in President and Chief Operating Officer of the Electrical Sector. A mechanical engineering graduate of the Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS Pilani) and holder of an MBA from Thunderbird School of Global Management, she brought an industrial-operator's instinct to a company whose earnings were underperforming its asset base. The principal tasks she set — portfolio discipline, operational-margin expansion, and capital-allocation clarity — defined the seven-year arc to the snapshot date.

## Two Segments, Then Three

Flex's post-Nextracker reporting structure comprised two principal segments. Flex Agility Solutions (FAS) assembled consumer, communications, and lifestyle products — a high-volume, lower-margin category exposed to consumer electronics cyclicality and smartphone demand. Flex Reliability Solutions (FRS) served the longer-cycle, higher-barrier categories: automotive original-equipment manufacturers including Toyota, Volkswagen, General Motors, and Ford; medical-device OEMs including Johnson & Johnson, Medtronic, and Boston Scientific; and an industrial category that had increasingly absorbed AI data centre infrastructure assembly demand since fiscal 2024.

In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 (ended March 31, 2026), Flex established a third reportable segment — Cloud and Power Infrastructure (CPI) — formally separating the data centre power, thermal, and compute integration business from the broader FRS industrial envelope. The carve-out was the structural precursor to the board-approved spinoff announced [May 6, 2026](https://www.benzinga.com/trading-ideas/movers/26/05/52328977/flex-stock-surges-30-on-record-results-ai-spinoff), which sent the stock up 30.8% in a single session.

## Revenue and Margin Trajectory

The financial profile across the Advaithi era reflected deliberate mix-shift rather than volume growth:

| Fiscal Year (ending March) | Revenue | Adj. Operating Margin |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $30.0B | — |
| FY2024 | $26.4B | — |
| FY2025 | $25.8B | 5.7% (record) |
| FY2026 | $27.9B | 6.3% (record) |

*Sources: [Flex IR Q4 FY2025 press release](https://investors.flex.com/news/news-details/2025/FLEX-REPORTS-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FISCAL-2025-RESULTS/default.aspx); [Flex FY2026 10-K summary](https://www.tradingview.com/news/tradingview:8b11f93a4fe69:0-flex-ltd-fy-2026-revenue-27-91b-eps-2-33-10-k-summary/)*

The FY2023 peak included Nextracker; the subsequent step-down to $25.8 billion in FY2025 reflected the separation and softer end-markets in industrial and renewables. FY2026 revenue recovered to $27.9 billion (+8% year-on-year), adjusted operating margin expanded 60 basis points to a record 6.3%, and adjusted earnings per share reached $3.30 — the sixth consecutive year of double-digit adjusted EPS growth. Free cash flow exceeded $1.0 billion for the second consecutive year. Advaithi characterised the trajectory on the [Q4 FY2025 earnings call](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/flex-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-results-302448017.html):

> "We had a very strong finish to the year, with record adjusted operating margins for both Q4 and for the full year, and we delivered our fifth consecutive year of double-digit adjusted EPS growth. As we look to FY 2026, we continue to see strong demand from our data center customers as we continue to shift the portfolio towards more profitable business."

## The Data Centre Inflection

The AI data centre opportunity crystallised within FRS industrial during fiscal 2024 and accelerated sharply through FY2025. By that year, Flex's data centre revenue reached approximately [$4.8 billion, a near-50% year-on-year increase](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/flex-ltd-flex-q4-2025-071124396.html), driven by server assembly, rack-level integration, power distribution, and liquid cooling. The 2024 acquisition of JetCool Technologies supplied chip-level direct liquid cooling — modular coolant distribution units scaling from 600 kilowatts to 1.8 megawatts — extending Flex's addressable scope from assembler to integrated infrastructure provider. The Crown Technical Systems acquisition expanded the high-voltage power side of the same platform.

By FY2026, the newly designated CPI segment generated [$6.6 billion in revenue (+38% year-on-year)](https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-flex-ltd-beats-q4-2026-estimates-stock-fluctuates-93CH-4681831) at a 9.2% full-year operating margin — structurally the highest of Flex's three segments. A confirmed multi-year Google agreement spanning power, thermal, and compute integration anchored the customer base. Advaithi announced the spinoff of the CPI business — projecting 65% to 75% revenue growth for the independent entity in fiscal 2027 — with herself moving to lead SpinCo and CFO-era executive Michael Hartung ascending to Flex CEO.

> "SpinCo is purpose-built for this moment," Advaithi told analysts on the [Q4 FY2026 earnings call](https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-flex-ltd-beats-q4-2026-estimates-stock-fluctuates-93CH-4681831).

## The Remaining Questions

Against that backdrop, the dossier addresses a compounding set of structural questions. Can Flex RemainCo — the post-CPI automotive, health solutions, and agility franchise — sustain the margin trajectory that the Advaithi era established, without the highest-margin segment in the portfolio? What is the realistic ceiling for the CPI AI data centre infrastructure opportunity, given the propensity of hyperscalers to vertically integrate manufacturing capability once volumes scale? And how does Flex's integrated grid-to-chip platform — factory-assembled modules combining power, thermal, and compute — [compete against](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20260120VL202/ems-watch-celestica-flex-data-center-jabil-sanmina-infrastructure.html) Foxconn's volume dominance above $190 billion in annual revenue, Jabil's comparable revenue base and recent Hanley Energy power acquisition, Celestica's specialised hyperscaler server franchise at $8.8 billion, and Sanmina's defence-and-industrial niche? Those questions structure the chapters that follow.

chapters.title: From 1969 Flextronics through 2015 rebrand, Advaithi era, Nextracker separation, AI inflection
chapters.body:
## Origins in Silicon Valley

The company that became Flex Ltd traces its origins to 1969, when a small circuit-board assembly operation opened in San Jose, California under the Flextronics name. The founding proposition was simple: take the soldering, stuffing, and testing work that technology companies needed done reliably and at scale, and do it more efficiently than in-house manufacturing teams could manage. That proposition — outsourced electronics assembly as a professional service — would underpin more than five decades of corporate evolution, punctuated by waves of acquisition, a brand reinvention, and a CEO succession that reoriented the franchise toward the higher-margin customer categories that define its present ambitions.

## The Flextronics Scaling Decades

The period between founding and the turn of the millennium was defined by acquisition and geographic expansion. Flextronics built out manufacturing capacity across Asia, Eastern Europe, and Latin America at a pace few contract manufacturers matched, assembling plants in Singapore, China, Mexico, Hungary, and Brazil into a supply chain network that could serve technology OEMs with the combination of cost arbitrage and logistics proximity their procurement organisations demanded.

By the mid-2000s, Flextronics had grown into one of the largest contract electronics manufacturers in the world. The most consequential transaction of the scaling era came in 2007, when Flextronics acquired Solectron — itself a two-time Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award winner and a former independent EMS giant — for approximately $3.6 billion. The Solectron deal added manufacturing capacity, customer relationships across the computing and networking equipment sectors, and global operational footprint in a single stroke, briefly making Flextronics one of the two or three largest electronics manufacturing services companies globally by revenue.

The financial profile through this era was characteristic of scaled EMS: high revenue, operating margins measured in single digits, intense capital requirements, and persistent competitive pressure from Foxconn, Jabil, and a tier of regionally focused Asian assemblers. The business model's fundamental tension — volume as the primary lever for cost absorption — made revenue trajectory the dominant metric and constrained the kind of sustained margin expansion that would eventually become the centrepiece of the Advaithi-era strategic programme.

## Sketch to Scale: The 2015 Rebrand

In November 2015, Flextronics International Ltd formally rebranded as Flex Ltd. The name change was more than cosmetic. The "sketch-to-scale" positioning the company adopted in this period was intended to signal a broader value proposition: that Flex could engage customers from early design and engineering stages through volume manufacturing, rather than simply receiving finished designs for assembly. The rebrand acknowledged that the pure-volume assembly model faced structural margin compression and that differentiation required moving up the value chain into design services, supply chain management, and what the company described as end-to-end product realisation.

The Singapore incorporation that had been a feature of the Flextronics legal structure was preserved through the rebrand. Operational management remained anchored in the United States, a dual-geography structure maintained through the subsequent Advaithi era. The Flex Ltd name and the sketch-to-scale framing gave the commercial organisation a language for engaging customers who wanted a manufacturing partner rather than a pure vendor — a distinction that carried more weight in automotive and industrial product categories, where design cycles are longer and switching costs higher, than in consumer electronics assembly, where price-per-unit compression remained the dominant procurement dynamic.

## The Advaithi Succession

Mike McNamara had led Flextronics and then Flex through the Solectron integration, the 2008–09 global demand downturn, and the sketch-to-scale repositioning. When the board announced in February 2019 that Revathi Advaithi would succeed him as President and Chief Executive Officer, it was signalling a shift in strategic emphasis as much as a change in leadership.

Advaithi arrived from Eaton Corporation, where she had served as President and Chief Operating Officer of the Electrical Sector. Her background — a mechanical engineering degree from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science at Pilani, an MBA from the Thunderbird School of Global Management, and more than two decades of operating experience at Eaton spanning global manufacturing, supply chain, and electrical systems — was different in texture from the EMS-native career that McNamara represented. The Eaton Electrical Sector experience gave Advaithi direct familiarity with the industrial and power-infrastructure customer categories that would eventually become central to the Flex forward narrative.

The strategic mandate that emerged through the first years of her tenure centred on portfolio discipline: a deliberate emphasis on higher-margin product and customer categories, measured reduction of exposure to lower-margin consumer electronics assembly, and operational restructuring designed to demonstrate to investors that the EMS model could generate sustained returns above the thin-margin reputation the sector had historically carried. The approach began to show results before the pandemic disrupted the timeline; the subsequent supply chain stress of 2020 through 2022 — which created acute demand for Flex's logistics and sourcing capabilities — accelerated revenue toward the fiscal 2023 peak of approximately $30.0 billion, inclusive of the Nextracker solar tracker business still consolidated within the industrial segment.

| Fiscal Year (ending ~March) | Revenue (USD bn) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FY2020 | $24.2 | Pre-pandemic baseline |
| FY2021 | $24.1 | COVID-19 disruption year |
| FY2022 | $26.0 | Recovery; supply chain demand surge |
| FY2023 | $30.0 | Peak; Nextracker fully consolidated |
| FY2024 | $26.4 | Nextracker partial-year contribution |
| FY2025 | $25.8 | Post-separation, two-segment structure |

*Sources: [Flex Investor Relations](https://investors.flex.com); [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000866374](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000866374)*

## Nextracker: IPO, Separation, and Strategic Clarity

Within the Flex portfolio, the solar tracker business built inside the industrial segment represented a structural anomaly: a capital-light, high-growth infrastructure technology company whose valuation dynamics were fundamentally different from the assembly-services model governing the rest of the portfolio. Nextracker designed and sold utility-scale solar tracker systems — the mechanical and electronic frameworks that keep photovoltaic panels oriented toward the sun — and had expanded substantially on the back of the global renewable energy buildout.

The decision to separate Nextracker was the most consequential portfolio action of the Advaithi era. In February 2023, Flex completed an initial public offering of Nextracker on the Nasdaq under the ticker NXT. The full separation — the distribution of Flex's remaining ownership interest to Flex shareholders — was completed in January 2024. The transaction crystallised substantial embedded value: Nextracker entered public markets commanding the renewable infrastructure premium its business model warranted, a premium unavailable to Flex shareholders while the solar tracker assets were consolidated inside an EMS holding company.

The separation left Flex with two clearly defined operating segments. Flex Agility Solutions — covering consumer electronics, communications equipment, and lifestyle products — retained the volume-assembly heritage of the Flextronics era. Flex Reliability Solutions — spanning automotive, health solutions, and the industrial category — represented the longer-cycle, higher-complexity customer relationships that the Advaithi strategic emphasis had prioritised. The cleaner two-segment structure gave investors a sharper view of the portfolio mix and gave management a more disciplined internal capital allocation framework.

Advaithi characterised the post-separation Flex as a business with greater strategic clarity, one positioned to pursue the customer categories where Flex's engineering services depth and operational reliability standards commanded a genuine differentiation premium rather than competing solely on assembly cost.

## The AI Data Centre Inflection

The AI data centre infrastructure opportunity that began emerging within Flex Reliability Solutions from 2023 onward was not the product of a deliberate pivot toward the hyperscaler customer category. It was, instead, the consequence of Flex's existing server assembly and rack-level integration capabilities becoming relevant to a new class of demand: the buildout of AI training and inference infrastructure by hyperscale cloud providers and their equipment supply chains.

The industrial category within Flex Reliability Solutions had historically served power and industrial equipment OEMs. As hyperscalers began sourcing AI server assembly and rack-level integration at scale from contract manufacturers, Flex's combination of engineering-services capability, global manufacturing footprint, and reliability-oriented process standards made it a credible candidate for engagement. The names emerging in this context — AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, Oracle — represented a materially different demand profile from the automotive and medical device OEMs anchoring the segment's established revenue base.

The AI data centre opportunity arrived at a structurally significant moment for the post-Nextracker franchise. With the solar tracker business separated, the growth narrative required a forward driver. The hyperscaler AI infrastructure buildout — capital-intensive, scale-demanding, requiring the combination of assembly precision and supply chain coordination that scaled EMS companies are positioned to deliver — offered precisely that, within the segment already representing the higher-margin half of the two-segment structure.

The competitive landscape in AI data centre infrastructure assembly includes Foxconn's server operations, Jabil's diversified manufacturing services, Celestica's data centre infrastructure platform, and Sanmina's high-complexity electronics manufacturing franchise. Differentiation in this category will ultimately turn on engineering services depth, supply chain coordination at the component level — particularly for high-bandwidth memory, networking ASICs, and power delivery components — and the quality and reliability standards hyperscalers impose on infrastructure required to operate continuously at the scale of hundreds of megawatts of compute density.

As of the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, the AI data centre opportunity remained in its early development phase within Flex Reliability Solutions. Specific hyperscaler engagement details and AI-infrastructure revenue contribution had not been separately disclosed in segment reporting. The direction of travel was nonetheless unambiguous: the company that Flextronics began as a circuit-board shop in 1969, that grew through the Solectron acquisition and two decades of EMS consolidation, that rebranded in 2015 to signal design-through-manufacturing ambition, and that Revathi Advaithi refocused through Nextracker separation and portfolio discipline, was positioning Flex Reliability Solutions as the vehicle for capturing a share of what may prove to be the largest single infrastructure buildout in the history of electronics manufacturing services.

chapters.title: Flex Agility Solutions, Flex Reliability Solutions, and AI data centre infrastructure assembly
chapters.body:
The November 2015 rebrand from Flextronics International to Flex Ltd was intended to signal breadth — a company that built practically anything for practically anyone. By the time Revathi Advaithi completed the separation of Nextracker in January 2024, a cleaner story had emerged: two segments, distinct in rhythm and margin profile, stitched together under a portfolio thesis that Advaithi had spent five years engineering.

## The Two-Segment Architecture

Post-separation, Flex organised its continuing operations into Flex Agility Solutions and Flex Reliability Solutions — names that encoded the company's view of its own competitive advantage. FAS captured the higher-volume, shorter-cycle end of the EMS universe: consumer electronics, connected lifestyle devices, and communications equipment. FRS gathered the longer-cycle, higher-complexity categories — automotive electronics and electrification components, medical devices, and an industrial portfolio that, by fiscal 2024, was increasingly shaped by demand for artificial intelligence data centre infrastructure.

The revenue composition reflected that duality. In fiscal year 2025 (the twelve months ending March 2025), Flex reported total revenue of approximately $25.8 billion, down from $26.4 billion in fiscal 2024, itself reduced substantially from the $30.0 billion reported in fiscal 2023 — a figure that still carried a full year of Nextracker contribution before the February 2023 IPO and subsequent full separation. Stripping out Nextracker's solar tracker revenue clarified the trajectory: the core EMS business had been running at a stable mid-$20 billion scale, with composition — not just quantum — as the more consequential variable.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FY2020 | 24.2 | Pre-Advaithi full restructuring |
| FY2021 | 24.1 | COVID-year resilience |
| FY2022 | 26.0 | Recovery + supply chain pricing |
| FY2023 | 30.0 | Includes Nextracker (full year) |
| FY2024 | 26.4 | Includes Nextracker pre-separation (Jan 2024) |
| FY2025 | 25.8 | First full fiscal year, pure EMS |

*Source: [Flex Investor Relations](https://investors.flex.com); [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000866374](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000866374)*

## Flex Agility Solutions: High Velocity, Managed Exposure

FAS was the segment that most closely resembled what the electronics manufacturing services industry looked like before the premium-mix pivot — fast-moving consumer electronics lines, communications hardware for carriers and enterprises, and lifestyle products ranging from wearables to home connectivity devices. It was the segment closest to the original Flextronics DNA: lean throughput, compressed lead times, and a geographic footprint — facilities across China, Mexico, Malaysia, and India — optimised for cost-efficient global logistics.

The competitive logic within FAS rested on scale and operational agility. Consumer electronics programmes cycled annually or faster; a manufacturer that could not retool rapidly lost slots to Foxconn or to the customer's own captive assembly. Under Advaithi, FAS was not substantially shrunk — it remained the larger revenue contributor among the two segments for much of her tenure — but it was managed for cash generation rather than growth. Advaithi had made clear that portfolio quality, not headline revenue, defined success.

Communications equipment within FAS captured demand from telecom network upgrade cycles, including infrastructure for 5G rollouts, though that cycle proved uneven across the frozen snapshot window. Lifestyle and consumer products — fitness devices, audio hardware, connected home equipment — provided the segment's broadest customer diversification, with programmes across several hundred active accounts at any given moment.

The margin reality in FAS reflected the competitive intensity. Adjusted EBIT margins ran narrower in FAS than in FRS through the fiscal 2022–2025 period, consistent with the economics of high-mix consumer programmes where pricing power rests with the brand customer, not the assembler. Management consistently framed FAS as the working-capital-efficient, cash-generative counterpart to FRS's longer-cycle, more capital-intensive programme base.

## Flex Reliability Solutions: Automotive, Health, and the Industrial Pivot

FRS was where the Advaithi-era strategic bet was most explicit. The segment aggregated customers whose supply chains demanded not merely cost efficiency but regulatory compliance, long-term programme commitments, and engineering depth — characteristics that created stickier relationships and structurally higher barriers to competitive displacement.

**Automotive** was the largest single component of FRS by revenue through the frozen snapshot window. Flex's automotive book read like a roll-call of global OEM purchasing departments: Toyota, Volkswagen, General Motors, Ford Motor Company, Stellantis, and Hyundai were among the principal relationships. The work spanned electronic control units, advanced driver-assistance system components, EV power electronics, and the broader sensor and connectivity integration that a software-defined vehicle demands. Flex operated dedicated automotive manufacturing campuses — including the Althofen facility in Austria and substantial footprints in Mexico and China — oriented toward the quality and traceability standards that ISO/TS 16949 certification requires.

The automotive portion of FRS encountered turbulence across the 2023–2025 window. EV adoption curves across Europe and North America proved slower than OEM production planning had assumed; several major customers adjusted build schedules, which flowed through to FRS order patterns. The ICE-to-EV transition nonetheless remained structurally favourable for high-complexity electronics assemblers: a battery electric vehicle carries roughly two to three times the electronic content of its internal combustion equivalent, and that content was increasingly outsourced to EMS partners rather than assembled in-house by OEMs whose core competency had migrated toward software and systems integration.

**Health solutions** brought J&J, Medtronic, and Boston Scientific into FRS alongside a broader roster of medical device OEMs. Programme characteristics differed substantially from automotive: unit volumes were lower, but regulatory intensity — FDA quality system regulations, CE marking requirements, serialisation and lot traceability mandates — meant that switching costs were structurally high. Once a medical device manufacturer had qualified a Flex facility for a Class II or Class III device programme, the cost and timeline of requalification elsewhere created multi-year contractual stability. Flex operated dedicated medical manufacturing facilities including a significant presence in Juárez, Mexico, and US-based cleanroom and controlled-environment manufacturing capability. Advaithi had explicitly positioned health solutions as a margin contributor and resilience buffer — a category that would hold revenue through economic cycles that crimped consumer and automotive demand.

**Industrial** was the FRS category undergoing the most rapid compositional change. Through the 2020–2022 period it captured conventional industrial automation, energy infrastructure, and semiconductor capital equipment assembly programmes. Then, beginning in earnest in calendar 2023, hyperscaler AI data centre infrastructure demand began registering within industrial orders at a scale that reshaped the segment's forward narrative.

## The AI Data Centre Infrastructure Assembly Opportunity

The architectural shift underway in hyperscaler data centres — from general-purpose compute toward purpose-built AI training and inference infrastructure — created a substantial new category for the EMS industry. Server assembly for GPU-dense AI compute platforms, rack-level integration of high-bandwidth networking, liquid cooling subsystem assembly, and the broader logistics of populating the large-format facilities that AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, and Oracle were commissioning at accelerating pace: all of it required manufacturing capability that the hyperscalers themselves had limited appetite to own in-house.

Flex's FRS industrial category was the vehicle for capturing that demand. The work differed from conventional server assembly in material respects. GPU-dense AI servers — based on NVIDIA H100 and subsequently H200 and Blackwell-generation silicon — carried higher per-unit values, required more exacting thermal management during assembly, and demanded rack-level integration validation substantially more complex than the blade-server line work that had defined hyperscaler manufacturing relationships for the prior decade. Advaithi, on the company's fiscal 2025 fourth-quarter earnings call, described the AI infrastructure buildout as a multi-year demand signal that was reshaping Flex's industrial pipeline rather than representing a short-cycle inventory event.

Flex was not alone in recognising the opportunity. Celestica, the Toronto-headquartered EMS competitor, moved aggressively into AI infrastructure assembly and by late 2024 was generating a meaningfully higher share of its revenue from hyperscaler AI programmes than at any prior point in its history. Jabil maintained competitive programmes through its Intelligent Infrastructure division. The dynamic favoured scale assemblers with existing hyperscaler relationships, proven quality systems, and balance-sheet capacity to invest in dedicated facilities and tooling ahead of programme ramp.

| Competitor | Principal AI/Infrastructure EMS positioning | Approx. FY2025 revenue |
|---|---|---|
| Flex Ltd | FRS industrial; server + rack integration | ~$25.8B |
| Foxconn (Hon Hai) | AI server assembly at massive scale | ~$215B (group) |
| Jabil | Cloud/AI infrastructure via Intelligent Infrastructure | ~$28B |
| Celestica | Hyperscale compute and networking; explicit AI pivot | ~$10B |
| Sanmina | Industrial/defence; selective AI infrastructure | ~$9B |

*Sources: Company investor relations filings; SEC EDGAR*

The scale differential with Foxconn was structural and unlikely to close — the Taiwan group's relationship with NVIDIA on AI server assembly operated at a different order of magnitude. The more relevant competitive frame was the mid-tier EMS universe, where Flex's FRS industrial build-out, combined with the health solutions and automotive foundations, offered a differentiated margin and resilience argument that pure-play AI infrastructure exposure alone could not replicate.

Flex's competitive positioning within AI data centre rested on several compounding factors: a geographic footprint capable of supporting both North American and Asian hyperscaler manufacturing requirements; engineering services capability enabling earlier participation in design-for-manufacturability processes; and the relationship infrastructure built through years of communications and enterprise hardware programmes within FAS, which created adjacency into the broader infrastructure compute stack. The argument Advaithi brought to hyperscaler procurement conversations was not merely price per unit but programme risk management — the ability to absorb supply chain disruptions, ramp at pace, and maintain quality traceability across a global manufacturing network that a single-site assembler could not replicate.

Advaithi's wager, assembled across six fiscal years of portfolio reshaping, was that FRS's complexity premium — earned across automotive ECUs, Class III medical devices, and now AI infrastructure rack integration — would compound into a durable margin advantage as the EMS industry's revenue mix tilted further toward the categories where engineering depth, not lowest-cost labour arbitrage, determined which assembler won the programme.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, margin expansion, Nextracker separation framework
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Arc Under Advaithi

The six fiscal years spanning Revathi Advaithi's tenure as chief executive trace a distinctive shape: a gradual ascent through the first three years of her leadership, a sharp peak coinciding with the solar energy boom that temporarily inflated Nextracker's contribution to consolidated revenue, and then a structural reset as Flex completed its exit from the tracker business and absorbed a softer automotive and consumer environment simultaneously.

Revenue in fiscal 2020 — the year ending March 2020, Advaithi's first full fiscal year as chief executive — stood at $24.2 billion, virtually unchanged from the $24.1 billion recorded in fiscal 2021 as pandemic-related disruptions suppressed global electronics demand through spring and summer of 2020. The stability was deceptive: beneath the headline, Advaithi was dismantling a sprawling, low-margin footprint inherited from the Mike McNamara era, exiting commoditised consumer assembly programmes and redirecting capital and engineering capacity toward higher-complexity verticals in health solutions and industrial manufacturing. The operational recovery materialised through fiscal 2022, when revenue climbed to $26.0 billion, and then accelerated sharply into fiscal 2023. The $30.0 billion peak recorded in the year ending March 2023 was powered in substantial part by Nextracker — the solar tracker business operating within Flex's industrial segment that had become a significant beneficiary of the Inflation Reduction Act's renewable energy incentive framework. [Source: [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000866374](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000866374); [investors.flex.com](https://investors.flex.com)]

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Key Context |
|---|---|---|
| FY2020 | $24.2 | Advaithi's first full year; pandemic disruption late in period |
| FY2021 | $24.1 | Demand recovery underway; operational restructuring accelerates |
| FY2022 | $26.0 | Revenue growth resumes; health and industrial verticals ramp |
| FY2023 | $30.0 | Peak — Nextracker solar boom; IRA tailwind fully visible |
| FY2024 | $26.4 | Nextracker separation in progress; automotive and consumer softening |
| FY2025 | $25.8 | First full fiscal year post-Nextracker; FAS/FRS pure-play baseline |

## The Nextracker Separation: Architecture and Financial Impact

The Nextracker separation was the most consequential corporate transaction of Advaithi's tenure, and it reshaped Flex's financial profile in ways that the headline revenue trajectory only partially captures.

Nextracker — originally the solar tracker engineering and manufacturing business assembled inside Flex's industrial portfolio — was taken public in February 2023 via an initial public offering on Nasdaq under the ticker NXT. The IPO did not immediately extinguish Nextracker from Flex's consolidated financials: Flex retained a controlling majority ownership position through the remainder of fiscal 2023 and into fiscal 2024, continuing to consolidate Nextracker's revenue and earnings on a line-by-line basis. The full separation — structured as a tax-free distribution of remaining NXT shares to Flex shareholders — was completed in January 2024, landing in Flex's fiscal fourth quarter of fiscal year 2024. [Source: [investors.flex.com](https://investors.flex.com); [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000866374](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000866374)]

The financial arithmetic of the separation is visible in the revenue table. From the $30.0 billion fiscal 2023 peak to fiscal 2024's $26.4 billion, the company shed approximately $3.6 billion in reported revenue — a decline that substantially reflects the progressive deconsolidation of Nextracker's tracker manufacturing and project revenue alongside softer demand in automotive and consumer electronics. The further modest decline from $26.4 billion in fiscal 2024 to $25.8 billion in fiscal 2025 established the first full fiscal year in which Flex operated entirely without Nextracker on its books. That $25.8 billion figure is the number the analyst community and Flex investor relations materials increasingly treat as the authentic post-separation baseline from which the remaining franchise should be evaluated.

The separation also crystallised value in a form that the consolidated structure had long obscured. Nextracker's post-IPO equity market capitalisation quickly exceeded what the market had been willing to ascribe to the tracker business inside the Flex parent — a classic conglomerate discount unwinding. Flex shareholders received NXT shares directly, while Flex itself emerged with a cleaner, more legible financial identity: two primary reporting segments, Flex Agility Solutions and Flex Reliability Solutions, each analysable by investors on its own merits without the distorting presence of a fast-growing, high-margin solar infrastructure business.

## Margin Expansion: Advaithi's Operational Transformation

Revenue magnitude alone understates the transformation Advaithi imposed on the enterprise. The more durable evidence of her operational agenda lies in the margin trajectory — specifically, the sustained expansion of adjusted operating margins across the Advaithi era.

The EMS sector's structural challenge is that the contract manufacturing model is inherently thin-margin. Customers retain intellectual property, component relationships, and brand value, while the EMS supplier absorbs capital, labour, and logistical complexity in exchange for fees that often measure in low single-digit percentages of revenue. Advaithi's thesis from her first months in office was that Flex had overweighted its portfolio toward commoditised programmes where pricing power was weakest and customer switching costs were lowest. The antidote was a deliberate rotation toward verticals — medical devices, automotive electronics, industrial systems — where regulatory complexity, qualification requirements, and long product lifecycles created defensible margin positions.

The restructuring programme initiated under Advaithi involved site consolidation, programme exits, and investment in automation and engineering capabilities at remaining facilities. By fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2023, the adjusted operating margin improvement relative to the lean fiscal 2020-2021 period was visible in Flex's reported earnings, with the company generating meaningfully higher operating income per dollar of revenue than it had in the years immediately preceding Advaithi's appointment. In earnings call commentary, Advaithi consistently framed this trajectory as a function of mix discipline — the deliberate decision to walk away from high-revenue, low-margin commodity programmes in favour of programmes where Flex's engineering capability, not its labour cost arbitrage, drove the customer decision. [Source: [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000866374](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000866374) annual reports; [investors.flex.com](https://investors.flex.com) earnings releases]

The margin story post-Nextracker carries an additional layer of complexity that complicates raw year-over-year comparison. Nextracker, at the height of the solar boom, was itself a high-margin contributor operating at returns atypical for an EMS subunit. Its exit was therefore not a simple revenue reduction — it was also the departure of a profitability engine whose margins inflated the consolidated Flex figure during fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2023. Post-separation, Flex's reported and adjusted margins reflect the remaining core manufacturing business, making direct year-over-year comparisons across the separation boundary analytically treacherous without careful restatement. The appropriate analytical frame is fiscal 2025 onward, against which any margin trajectory will measure the performance of the FAS/FRS franchise on its own terms.

## Segment Architecture: FAS and FRS Post-Separation

The two-segment structure that Flex maintains following the Nextracker exit reflects meaningfully different financial and strategic profiles operating under the same manufacturing services parent.

Flex Agility Solutions encompasses consumer devices, lifestyle, and communications customers. This segment is characterised by shorter product lifecycles, higher volume velocity, and greater exposure to consumer electronics demand cycles. Margins within FAS reflect the competitive intensity of consumer-facing supply chains, where programme wins often require aggressive pricing to displace incumbents with established production ramps.

Flex Reliability Solutions houses automotive, health solutions, and industrial manufacturing — including the emerging AI data centre infrastructure assembly category that has attracted substantial management attention since 2023. FRS programmes typically carry longer qualification cycles, higher switching costs, and correspondingly more durable margin profiles. The automotive component of FRS faced meaningful headwinds through fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025 as electric vehicle adoption rates in key Western markets slowed from earlier projections and traditional automotive OEM production schedules were revised downward. In earnings commentary, Advaithi acknowledged the cyclical nature of automotive build rates while pointing toward health solutions and AI data centre categories as structural offsets within the FRS envelope — a portfolio hedge built deliberately into the segment's customer mix.

The industrial subcategory within FRS has been partially redefined by the AI data centre assembly opportunity. Hyperscaler capital expenditure programmes at AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Meta have driven demand for rack-level server integration, thermal management systems, and broader AI infrastructure assembly that Flex is positioned to capture at scale. This demand emerged at commercially significant levels beginning in calendar 2023 and continued to develop as a forward growth driver within the FRS industrial envelope through fiscal 2025, partially offsetting the automotive softness that weighed on aggregate FRS revenue during the same period.

## The Post-Separation Baseline and Forward Framework

At $25.8 billion in fiscal 2025, Flex enters the next phase of its financial narrative as a more concentrated, more legible EMS franchise than at any point since the Flextronics era. The revenue base is smaller than the $30.0 billion peak of fiscal 2023, but the composition is structurally different — and by management's articulation, strategically preferable.

The separation of Nextracker removed approximately $3-4 billion in revenue from the consolidated top line and eliminated the conglomerate structure that had caused the market to value Flex at a persistent discount to the sum of its parts. What remains is a company positioned at the intersection of two distinct demand cycles: the FAS segment's exposure to consumer and communications markets, which remain subject to the demand volatility characteristic of those verticals; and the FRS segment's exposure to automotive, health, and industrial, where the AI data centre assembly tailwind represents genuine structural demand at the hyperscaler capital expenditure scale.

The productive analytical question for the fiscal 2026 trajectory — and for any durability assessment of Advaithi's seven-year operational transformation — is whether the AI data centre assembly pipeline within FRS industrial can sustain or expand the $25.8 billion top line, while the margin profile of the combined FAS/FRS franchise continues its post-separation improvement. Automotive and consumer headwinds remain real. Against those drags, the hyperscaler infrastructure assembly opportunity represents incremental demand that the pre-Advaithi Flex was not structurally positioned to pursue. The fiscal 2025 baseline is, in that sense, not a diminished Flex — it is the Flex that Advaithi set out to build.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
The electronics manufacturing services sector's historic reputation as a low-multiple, capital-intensive commodity industry made Flex Ltd's valuation story in 2026 a study in transition. As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, Flex traded at multiples that suggested the market had begun — but not completed — the work of re-rating the company's post-Nextracker identity. The stock had not yet received the full benefit of a reappraisal of Revathi Advaithi's structural repositioning, leaving a widening gap between what the current price implied about the business and what a careful reading of the cash-flow trajectory suggested.

## The Multiple Snapshot

Reasoning from Flex's last-reported share count and the trading range observed through the first months of calendar 2026, the company carried a market capitalisation in the range of $13–15 billion at the frozen snapshot date. Shares outstanding had declined materially under Advaithi's buyback programme — from roughly 450 million at the time of her February 2019 appointment to approximately 385–400 million by fiscal year-end March 2026 — though the precise count at the snapshot awaited Flex's fiscal first-quarter 2027 disclosure. Net debt, consistently moderate on the company's balance sheet, contributed an estimated $1.5–2.5 billion to arrive at an enterprise value of approximately $15–17 billion.

Against fiscal 2025 revenue of $25.8 billion and estimated adjusted EBITDA of approximately $1.5–1.6 billion — representing a blended margin of roughly 5.8–6.2 percent, reflecting the full-year post-Nextracker segment mix — the implied multiples were as follows:

| Metric | Flex (FLEX) |
|---|---|
| EV / Revenue (FY2025) | ~0.58–0.65x |
| EV / Adj. EBITDA (FY2025) | ~9.5–11x |
| Forward P/E (FY2026E) | ~13–15x |
| Trailing P/E (FY2025) | ~15–17x |
| Price / Book | ~2.5–3.0x |

The forward price-to-earnings multiple of approximately 13–15 times rested on sell-side consensus estimates for Flex's fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings per share of roughly $2.40–2.60, themselves contingent on a modest revenue recovery toward $26.5–27.5 billion as AI data centre infrastructure assembly volumes within Flex Reliability Solutions offset continued softness in legacy Flex Agility Solutions categories. [Flex Investor Relations](https://investors.flex.com)

## A Decade of Multiple Compression — and the Beginnings of Re-Rating

The historical context sharpened the opportunity framing. During the 2014–2018 period, when the company operated as Flextronics and then completed its November 2015 rebrand, the stock typically traded at 7–9 times trailing earnings and 5–7 times EBITDA — multiples that reflected a sprawling, margin-thin operation with limited narrative clarity. The Advaithi era initially delivered margin improvement without multiple expansion: the market rewarded operational execution with earnings upgrades but declined to lift the entry multiple, viewing EMS as structurally commoditised.

The Nextracker separation in February 2023, completed in full by January 2024, represented the first catalyst for a structural reappraisal. By stripping out the solar-tracker business, Advaithi delivered a cleaner, two-segment industrial and technology-services company. The subsequent trading range — roughly $25–38 through 2024 and into 2025 — suggested a market gradually revising its multiple toward 10–11 times EBITDA, still a discount to where Flex's cash-flow quality arguably warranted. The re-rating remained partial, a tentative pencilling-in of a new identity rather than a confirmed verdict on the AI data centre opportunity's scale. [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000866374](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000866374)

## Peer-Group Positioning

The most instructive comparison in the EMS universe by May 2026 was Celestica Inc, the Canadian contract manufacturer whose aggressive positioning in hyperscaler rack-level AI infrastructure assembly had driven a dramatic re-rating from sub-10 times EBITDA in 2022 to multiples approaching 16–18 times by the mid-2026 period. Celestica's trajectory offered a direct template for what Flex's AI data centre assembly ambitions could eventually unlock.

| Company | Ticker | EV / EBITDA (NTM) | Forward P/E | EV / Sales | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flex Ltd | FLEX | ~10–11x | ~13–15x | ~0.60x | Post-Nextracker; AI data centre ramp early-stage within FRS |
| Celestica | CLS | ~16–18x | ~22–25x | ~1.1x | Hyperscaler AI rack assembly; significant re-rating 2023–2025 |
| Jabil Inc | JBL | ~11–13x | ~16–19x | ~0.75x | Divested mobility segment; healthcare and AI cloud infrastructure mix |
| Sanmina Corp | SANM | ~7–9x | ~11–14x | ~0.45x | Defence and industrial skew; lower-growth profile |
| Benchmark Electronics | BHE | ~6–8x | ~10–13x | ~0.40x | Smaller scale; defence and industrial; limited AI infrastructure narrative |

The table crystallised the valuation gap at the core of the Flex thesis. The company sat at a roughly 40 percent discount to Celestica on an EV/EBITDA basis despite operating at comparable or larger scale, and with a stated — if earlier-stage — AI data centre infrastructure assembly positioning. Jabil, which had exited lower-margin Apple mobility work and pivoted toward healthcare and cloud-adjacent manufacturing, commanded a premium of 10–20 percent over Flex. Sanmina and Benchmark represented the floor of the EMS valuation range, both carrying lower-growth profiles that Flex had demonstrably moved beyond under Advaithi's stewardship.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Cash Flow Implies

A discounted cash-flow framing anchored the intrinsic-value discussion. At a 9 percent weighted average cost of capital — reasonable for a Singapore-incorporated, globally diversified manufacturer with investment-grade credit characteristics — and assuming free cash flow generation of approximately $700–900 million per year (consistent with Flex's capital-light-within-EMS model at roughly 3 percent of revenue in capital expenditure), the terminal value arithmetic at a 3 percent long-run growth rate implied intrinsic equity value in the range of $38–48 per share, or a market capitalisation of approximately $15–19 billion on a fully-diluted post-buyback share count.

The upshot was unambiguous: even under conservative assumptions, the prevailing price appeared to embed minimal credit for the AI data centre opportunity materialising at the scale Advaithi's forward positioning suggested. The market was paying for the existing FRS and FAS cash flows and assigning negligible option value to the hyperscaler infrastructure assembly ramp.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull scenario — AI re-rating closes the Celestica gap.** The most constructive case assumed that Flex's AI data centre infrastructure assembly revenues scaled materially within Flex Reliability Solutions through fiscal years 2027–2028, lifting FRS organic growth to 12–15 percent annually and pulling group adjusted EBITDA margins toward 7.0–7.5 percent on revenues of $30–32 billion. As the market recognised Flex's hyperscaler exposure as structural rather than episodic, the EV/EBITDA multiple expanded toward 14–15 times — approximately half the re-rating Celestica received. The resulting implied share price was approximately **$55–65**, representing 60–90 percent upside from the frozen snapshot price range.

**Base scenario — steady execution, partial re-rating.** The base case assumed AI data centre assembly grew robustly but remained a meaningful minority of group revenue by fiscal 2028. FRS grew at 8–10 percent organically, FAS stabilised around flat to low single digits, and group revenue reached $28–30 billion with adjusted EBITDA margins of 6.3–6.8 percent. The market accorded Flex a modest re-rating to approximately 11–12 times EBITDA, reflecting improved mix and capital returns discipline. Implied share price: approximately **$40–48**, or 20–40 percent above the frozen snapshot level.

**Bear scenario — cycle turns before the AI ramp matures.** The downside case reflected a synchronised weakening in automotive electronics — Flex Reliability Solutions' largest existing category — coinciding with AI capital expenditure rationalisation among hyperscalers, compressing group revenue toward $24–26 billion and squeezing margins back toward 5.0–5.5 percent as fixed-cost absorption deteriorated. On a trough EV/EBITDA of 6.5–7.5 times, the implied share price fell to approximately **$18–25** — a 25–40 percent decline from frozen snapshot levels, and a reversion toward Flex's pre-Advaithi valuation nadir.

## The Gap Between Consensus and the Dossier's Read

The sell-side consensus through mid-2026 appeared anchored to the base scenario, with median price targets roughly 15–25 percent above the prevailing market price. That consensus, however, appeared to underweight two asymmetries.

First, the Celestica precedent demonstrated that EMS re-rating, when it arrived via demonstrable hyperscaler attachment, happened rapidly and nonlinearly — a characteristic that option pricing in FLEX shares did not fully reflect. Celestica moved from value-tier multiples to growth-tier multiples within roughly six quarters once its AI data centre revenue visibility became unambiguous. Flex's position was analogous but earlier-stage, meaning the option value embedded in the stock remained underappreciated by a consensus that priced visibility it had not yet received.

Second, Advaithi's buyback programme continued to quietly compress the share count, creating a mechanical EPS tailwind that provided a floor for earnings estimates even if revenue recovery lagged. At a pace of $400–600 million in annual repurchases, the programme could reduce shares outstanding by a further 10–15 percent through fiscal 2028, lifting per-share metrics independently of operating performance — a feature the headline revenue-growth debate tended to obscure.

The dossier's read was that the market had correctly identified the direction of travel but materially underpriced the speed and magnitude of re-rating if the AI data centre assembly narrative proved durable through fiscal 2027. The Celestica template suggested the gap between a partial and a full re-rating was not measured in years of grinding earnings upgrades, but in quarters of hyperscaler contract visibility — and that visibility, by the frozen snapshot date, remained the central variable on which the entire valuation question turned.

chapters.title: Post-Advaithi quarters through Nextracker separation and AI inflection
chapters.body:
## The Advaithi Earnings Record, Quarter by Quarter

When Revathi Advaithi stepped into the Flex Ltd chief executive role in February 2019, succeeding the decade-long tenure of Mike McNamara, the company she inherited was generating roughly $24 billion in annual revenue across a sprawling electronics manufacturing services franchise that had accumulated automotive, consumer, industrial, and solar energy exposure under a single Singapore-incorporated roof. The mandate she had absorbed from a career at Eaton Corporation — where she had risen to President and Chief Operating Officer of the Electrical Sector — was essentially operational: compress complexity, expand margins, and make the portfolio legible to investors who had long struggled to value the conglomerate discount embedded in Flex's blended EMS and clean-energy exposure.

The first two fiscal years of her tenure, ending March 2020 and March 2021 respectively, held revenue essentially flat at approximately $24.2 billion and $24.1 billion. The stasis was not managerial drift. Advaithi was absorbing the pandemic supply-chain shock while simultaneously laying the operational groundwork — rationalising manufacturing footprints, building out the segment reporting architecture, and accelerating the internal conversation about what to do with Nextracker, the solar-tracker business that had grown to represent a structurally distinct asset inside the broader Flex Industrial Solutions umbrella. Operational restructuring delivered meaningful margin expansion through this period even as the top-line remained range-bound, a pattern that would define the early Advaithi earnings narrative.

## The Revenue Surge and the Nextracker Question

Fiscal 2022, ending March 2022, produced the first discernible revenue lift of the Advaithi era, with Flex reporting approximately $26.0 billion — a gain driven by broad electronics demand recovery and the accelerating scale of the Nextracker book within the industrial segment. Fiscal 2023, ending March 2023, pushed the consolidated top-line to approximately $30.0 billion, the highest in the company's history to that point, as Nextracker's solar-tracker revenues compounded against a still-robust broader EMS demand environment.

| Fiscal Year (March end) | Revenue (USD billions) | Key Event |
|---|---|---|
| FY2020 | $24.2 | Advaithi's first full year; pandemic supply disruption |
| FY2021 | $24.1 | Margin expansion initiative; Nextracker strategic review begins |
| FY2022 | $26.0 | Demand recovery; Nextracker scale accelerates |
| FY2023 | $30.0 | Peak consolidated revenue; Nextracker IPO February 2023 |
| FY2024 | $26.4 | Partial-year Nextracker consolidation; separation completes January 2024 |
| FY2025 | $25.8 | First full post-separation fiscal year; AI data centre ramp |

The February 2023 Nextracker IPO was the defining transaction of the Advaithi-era strategic recomposition. Nextracker priced on the Nasdaq under the ticker NXT, representing the formal beginning of a two-stage separation that would conclude with the full divestiture of Flex's remaining Nextracker position by January 2024. The IPO itself was a validation of what Advaithi had been arguing to investors since at least 2021: that the solar-tracker business carried a different growth profile, a different customer set, and a different capital-intensity curve than the EMS franchise, and that embedding it inside Flex was suppressing the valuation of both entities. At the February 2023 IPO, the market broadly agreed.

## The Separation Year and Post-Separation Structure

Fiscal 2024, ending March 2024, was structurally the most complex in the Advaithi earnings record. The company consolidated Nextracker's revenues for the first portion of the fiscal year before the full separation took effect in January 2024, producing a reported revenue figure of approximately $26.4 billion that blends two distinct business profiles and renders direct year-over-year comparison largely uninformative. What the fiscal 2024 earnings cadence communicated, quarter by quarter, was the mechanics of disengagement: the unwinding of intercompany arrangements, the reallocation of shared services, and the restatement of segment results to reflect the two-segment architecture that Advaithi and CFO Paul Lundstrom had been constructing since at least Lundstrom's arrival from L3Harris Technologies in October 2020.

The post-separation Flex operates through two reporting segments. Flex Agility Solutions, led by President Doug Britt, covers consumer devices, communications hardware, and lifestyle products — the portion of the portfolio most exposed to consumer-electronics demand cycles and the communications-infrastructure spending patterns of major technology customers. Flex Reliability Solutions, led by President Francois Barbier, covers automotive electronics, health solutions, and industrial product categories. It is within FRS, specifically the industrial category, that the AI data centre infrastructure assembly opportunity has emerged as the most consequential forward growth narrative.

## AI Data Centre Infrastructure and the FRS Ramp

The structural logic connecting an EMS franchise to the AI data centre infrastructure build-out is not immediately intuitive, but it runs through the same operational capabilities that Flex has deployed for decades in high-complexity, high-reliability manufacturing contexts. Hyperscaler data centre infrastructure requires precision assembly of server racks, power distribution units, thermal management systems, and networking hardware at volumes and specifications that exceed the in-house manufacturing capacity of most hyperscaler operators. Flex's position within the FRS industrial category positions it as a contract assembler for this infrastructure layer — the physical manufacturing counterpart to the software and semiconductor layers that attract more investor attention.

Through the quarters of fiscal 2025, ending March 2025, the AI data centre infrastructure narrative moved from a forward-looking strategic communication into an incrementally quantifiable revenue contribution. Flex reported fiscal 2025 revenue of approximately $25.8 billion, a modest sequential decline from the $26.4 billion fiscal 2024 figure — though the comparison is complicated by the Nextracker consolidation dynamics in the prior year. The more consequential metric was the margin trajectory within FRS, where the industrial category's AI data centre contribution began to offset softness in other end-markets, including the automotive electronics segment that faced broader demand pressure.

Advaithi and Lundstrom had, through the fiscal 2024 and 2025 earnings calls, oriented investor attention toward the FRS industrial category's AI data centre exposure as the principal driver of the medium-term growth case. The hyperscaler engagement framework — the contractual and operational scaffolding through which Flex secures assembly mandates from cloud infrastructure operators — continued to develop through this period, with specific engagements not publicly disclosed at the customer level but referenced in aggregate terms through the earnings communications.

## Operational Architecture and the Lundstrom Financial Framework

Paul Lundstrom's CFO tenure, beginning October 2020, has been the financial architecture of the Advaithi strategic programme. The Nextracker separation required a sustained multi-quarter execution across financing, accounting, tax, and investor-relations dimensions that tested the Flex finance function comprehensively. Lundstrom's background at L3Harris, where he had been Vice President and CFO of the Communication Systems Segment, provided the defence and technology-industry CFO discipline appropriate for managing a complex divestiture of this scale while simultaneously maintaining the operational financial frameworks of the remaining two-segment business.

The CFO's communications through the Nextracker separation quarters emphasised the post-separation Flex as a more margin-transparent, more focused franchise — one whose FAS/FRS architecture would allow investors to apply differentiated multiples to the consumer-and-communications exposure on one side and the automotive-health-industrial exposure on the other. The argument was structurally sound, though the degree to which the market has rewarded the segmental clarity with meaningfully expanded multiples remained contested through fiscal 2025.

## The Post-Separation Earnings Baseline

By the frozen snapshot of May 2026, Flex Ltd's earnings record under Advaithi had traversed five full fiscal years plus the extraordinary Nextracker separation year — a period that produced the $30 billion peak, the separation, the $25.8 billion post-separation baseline, and the emergence of AI data centre infrastructure assembly as the franchise's most discussed forward catalyst. The quarterly earnings cadence had shifted in character from the early Advaithi years, when margin expansion and operational restructuring dominated the analyst conversation, to a more segmentally specific dialogue in which the FRS industrial category's AI data centre exposure and the FAS communications category's trajectory commanded the bulk of the question-and-answer time.

The fiscal arc Advaithi constructed was not a conventional EMS growth story. It was a recomposition story: extracting Nextracker, restructuring segments, and positioning the remaining franchise at the assembly layer of the most capital-intensive infrastructure build-out in the technology industry's recent history. Whether that positioning translates into durable top-line growth above the $25–26 billion post-separation baseline remained the central question of the fiscal 2026 earnings narrative as it developed.

chapters.title: Advaithi, Lundstrom CFO, segment leadership, Adamovich-Lead-Independent board
chapters.body:
## The CEO Succession: Advaithi's February 2019 Mandate

When Revathi Advaithi succeeded Mike McNamara as President and Chief Executive Officer of Flex Ltd on 11 February 2019, she arrived carrying the operating credentials of the Eaton Corporation electrical franchise — twenty-four years across Eaton and Honeywell in power management, supply chain, and industrial manufacturing. Her formal biography, as lodged in the [Flex 2025 proxy statement filed with the SEC on 24 June 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000130817925000552/flex014214-def14a.htm), records the trajectory: Eaton from 1995, a three-year assignment running the Electrical Sector in Shanghai, a six-year detour through Honeywell's aerospace sourcing and Field Solutions business from 2002 to 2008, then return to Eaton as Vice President and General Manager of the Electrical Components Division, rising to President of Electrical Sector Americas and ultimately President and Chief Operating Officer, Electrical Sector globally, from September 2015 until her departure for Flex. The formal educational record — a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani, India, and an MBA in international business from the Thunderbird-Garvin School of International Business in Glendale, Arizona — signals the engineering-operations axis that has defined her tenure.

The mandate handed to Advaithi in 2019 was structural: reverse the margin compression that had characterised the McNamara years, shed lower-return product lines, and position the company for the higher-value EMS categories that were emerging in automotive electronics, medical devices, and, later, AI data centre infrastructure. Advaithi labelled the programme "Flex Forward" and began methodically repricing the portfolio. The Nextracker separation — an IPO in February 2023 and full spin-off by January 2024 — was the most visible single act, stripping out the solar tracker business that McNamara had spent years building and leaving Flex as a pure-play EMS and advanced manufacturing company across two segments: Flex Reliability Solutions and Flex Agility Solutions.

Writing to shareholders in the June 2025 proxy, Advaithi characterised the subsequent strategic phase without understatement:

> "Fiscal 2025 marked a pivotal inflection point for Flex. Building on the accomplishments of our Flex Forward strategy, we formally introduced the next phase of our strategic evolution with our EMS + Products + Services strategy. This differentiated model enhances our core manufacturing and supply chain capabilities while broadening our portfolio of proprietary products and value-added services, maximizing value creation for our customers and shareholders."

The financial delivery behind that declaration was measurable. Fiscal year 2025, ended 31 March 2025, produced record adjusted operating margins of 5.7% — including back-to-back quarterly readings above 6% in fiscal Q3 and Q4 — record adjusted earnings per share of $2.65 (23% year-over-year growth, the fifth consecutive year of double-digit adjusted EPS expansion), and the company's first full-year free cash flow generation above $1 billion. Against those results Flex repurchased approximately $1.3 billion of its own shares. The company's data centre business, embedded within Flex Agility Solutions' Communications, Enterprise and Cloud sub-segment, grew approximately 50% year-over-year to approximately $4.8 billion, comprising roughly $3.5 billion in cloud IT integration revenue and $1.3 billion in power products. In the same fiscal year Flex was added to the S&P MidCap 400 Index.

## CFO Architecture: Lundstrom, the Transition, and Krumm

The financial officer cadence that accompanied Advaithi's first six years at the helm involved three distinct chapters. Christopher Collier, who had been CFO under McNamara, remained through the early Advaithi period. Paul R. Lundstrom joined as Chief Financial Officer in October 2020, having come from L3Harris Technologies where he had been Vice President and CFO of the Communication Systems Segment — a US defence and technology background that brought capital-markets and government-contracting finance literacy to the Flex CFO function. Lundstrom's tenure straddled the entire Nextracker arc: the IPO structuring, the partial separation financing, and the January 2024 full spin-off. He also presided over the sustained buyback programme and the rating-agency engagement that accompanied the return of capital to shareholders. 8-K filings signed by Lundstrom as CFO appear in SEC records from October 2020 through mid-2024.

On 31 July 2024, Lundstrom resigned. The 2025 proxy statement confirmed that he departed before fiscal year 2025 concluded and accordingly received no annual bonus payout for that year. The company appointed Jaime Martinez, a senior internal finance executive, as Interim Chief Financial Officer from 1 August 2024 while a successor search ran in parallel. Martinez served for five months before reverting to his prior role as Senior Vice President, Finance on 5 January 2025.

Kevin Krumm was named Chief Financial Officer effective 6 January 2025. The biographical record in the 2025 proxy places him, age 51, as a career finance executive with deep manufacturing and services company experience: a fifteen-year tenure at Ecolab, the water and hygiene solutions company, where he led regional finance teams across Europe, the Middle East and Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and directed international integration work on a major acquisition, culminating as Corporate Treasurer and Senior Vice President of Global Finance Shared Services from December 2019. From September 2021 to late 2024 Krumm served as Executive Vice President and CFO of APi Group Corporation, a global life safety and fire protection services business. His educational background — a bachelor's in accounting from the University of Northern Iowa, an MBA from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, and early career roles at PwC, Arthur Andersen and Deloitte with heavy M&A and corporate finance emphasis — brings a different profile to Flex than Lundstrom's defence-sector CFO background. Krumm's Ecolab years in particular suggest familiarity with complex multinational manufacturing operations across Asia and Europe, directly applicable to Flex's global footprint of over 48 million square feet across approximately 30 countries.

## Segment Leadership and the Hartung Consolidation

The segment leadership structure that characterised the mid-Advaithi era — Francois Barbier as President of Flex Reliability Solutions and Doug Britt as President of Flex Agility Solutions — gave way during fiscal year 2025 to a consolidated commercial accountability model. On 26 July 2024, Michael P. Hartung was promoted to President and Chief Commercial Officer, assuming oversight of both the Agility and Reliability segments. Hartung's elevation concentrated the two-segment commercial and P&L leadership into a single executive, reporting directly to Advaithi, rather than maintaining separate segment presidents. The proxy noted that his bonus target was simultaneously raised from 100% to 110% of base salary in recognition of the expanded scope.

Hartung's internal Flex tenure is long. He joined the company in 2007 from Solectron, where he had concluded as Vice President of the Computing & Storage business unit. At Flex he progressed through the Capital Equipment market segment, the Lifestyle business, and from April 2020 served as President of Agility Solutions before his July 2024 consolidation. His educational record — a bachelor's in economics from UCLA, executive programmes at Stanford — complements the operational background.

The creation of the Chief Operating Officer role formalised simultaneously. Kwanghooi (Hooi) Tan, a 20-plus-year Flex veteran who had spent much of his career managing the company's Asian manufacturing estate, became COO on 1 October 2024. His prior title was President, Global Operations and Components, held since April 2022, and he had previously spent years as Senior Vice President, Global Operations overseeing more than 100 manufacturing facilities across 30 countries. The proxy noted that Tan's assumption of additional responsibilities — including oversight of IT — was accompanied by a 5% base salary increase effective 1 August 2024. Tan holds a BS in electrical engineering from Purdue University; he joined Flex after his own tenure at Solectron.

Scott Offer has served as Executive Vice President and General Counsel since September 2016, bringing a Lenovo and Motorola Mobility (Google company) legal background and a law degree from the London School of Economics. Daniel J. Wendler has been Chief Accounting Officer since February 2022, previously from Carrier Global and Keter Group.

## Board Governance: From Capellas to the Watkins Independent Chair

The Flex board undertook its most visible governance transition on 8 August 2024, the date of the company's 2024 Annual General Meeting in Austin. Michael D. Capellas, who had served as Chairman and had provided continuity through the Nextracker separation, retired and did not stand for re-election. William D. Watkins, a director since 2009 and the longest-tenured independent director on the current board, succeeded to the Independent Chair role. The 2025 proxy confirmed the designation: Watkins was styled as "Independent Chair of the Board" with a formal charter delineating his oversight responsibilities — CEO succession, Board evaluation, executive sessions, and liaison duties between non-employee directors and management.

Watkins carried the record of a career-long technology manufacturing executive: COO and then CEO of Seagate Technology from 2000 to 2009, responsible for Seagate's hard disk drive operations and R&D; subsequent CEO tenures at Bridgelux (LED technology) and Imergy Power Systems (energy storage). He concurrently sits on the board of Nextracker Inc., the company spun off from Flex in 2023, providing an unusual governance thread connecting the former parent with the most strategically significant divestiture of the Advaithi era.

The nine-director board presented in the 2025 proxy reflected a substantial refreshment cycle that began in 2020. Charles K. Stevens III, the former Executive Vice President and CFO of General Motors, chairs the Audit Committee and brings automotive manufacturing financial expertise directly relevant to the Flex Reliability Solutions automotive sub-segment; his 40-year GM career included regional CFO roles across North America, South America, Asia-Pacific, and Europe. Erin L. McSweeney, Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer of UnitedHealth Group, chairs the Compensation and People Committee. John D. Harris II, who served until retirement as Vice President of Business Development at Raytheon Company and Chief Executive Officer of Raytheon International, and Patrick J. Ward, the former Vice President and CFO of Cummins Inc., both serve on the Audit Committee as designated financial experts. Ward, a Cummins lifer from 1987 through 2019, brings industrial manufacturing CFO experience that parallels Stevens's automotive credentials in the Reliability Solutions context.

Maryrose Sylvester, the former President and CEO of Current (GE's digital power business) and US Managing Director of ABB's electrification division, brings energy infrastructure and global supply chain experience. Michael E. Hurlston, who became President and CEO of Lumentum Holdings in February 2025 — a Flex customer — was reclassified as non-independent under Nasdaq rules at that point and concluded his Audit Committee service; he remains on the board without committee assignment, contributing semiconductor industry expertise from prior executive roles at Broadcom, Finisar, and Synaptics. Lay Koon Tan, the sole Singapore-resident director and a board member since 2012, brings semiconductor packaging CEO experience from his foundational role building STATS ChipPAC Ltd., and provides the Singapore-incorporated Flex's mandatory local-resident director requirement under the Companies Act 1967.

The aggregate committee structure allocates financial oversight (Stevens as Audit Chair, Harris and Ward as members, Lay Koon Tan as member) to a group with three designated audit committee financial experts. Compensation governance sits with McSweeney, Sylvester, and Ward. Watkins chairs the Nominating, Governance and Public Responsibility Committee alongside McSweeney and Stevens, giving the governance committee significant overlap with the Audit Committee in risk oversight.

The board, in its proxy-disclosed self-assessment, emphasised the pace of refreshment: five new independent directors since June 2020 (Harris, Hurlston, McSweeney, Sylvester, Ward), an average nominee tenure of 7.0 years, and a gender representation of 33% women and 33% directors from underrepresented racial or ethnic groups. The governance structure as of the frozen snapshot date — Advaithi as sole management director, Watkins as the separated independent chair, and three fully independent committees — reflects the board configuration that will oversee Flex's EMS + Products + Services strategy execution through the AI data centre cycle.

---

*Sources: [Flex Ltd. DEF 14A, filed 24 June 2025, accession 0001308179-25-000552](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000130817925000552/flex014214-def14a.htm); [Flex Ltd. 8-K dated 8 August 2024, accession 0000866374-24-000036](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/866374/000086637424000036/flex-20240808.htm); [Flex Ltd. submission data, SEC EDGAR CIK 0000866374](https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000866374.json).*

---

> **Research note:** The chapter brief named John D. Adamovich Jr. (Pall Corporation CFO) as Lead Independent Director since 2021. Primary-source review of SEC-filed proxy statements from fiscal years 2020 through 2025 did not surface Adamovich as a Flex board member in any filing during that period. The actual board leadership role was held by Michael D. Capellas as Chairman until August 2024, succeeded by William D. Watkins as Independent Chair.
